turns.prompt_text: Okay, so we pulled some comb off of a hive and it has a lot of drone brood and drone larvae in it and all that comb. So because we have all this comb we want to melt it down into wax but because there's a larvae in nearly every single hexagon We don't know how to properly separate these two One solution I thought was that the larvae would essentially become carbon
turns.response_html:
Dealing with a high volume of drone brood in comb you want to render down is a common scenario, especially if you're practicing drone brood removal for varroa mite management.

Your intuition about the larvae becoming carbon makes sense on the surface—heat organic matter enough, and it burns down to carbon. However, in practice, trying to vaporize or char the larvae while saving the wax won't work. Organic tissue is mostly water and protein. If you heat the mixture high enough to char the larvae, you will completely burn, discolor, and ruin the beeswax long before the larvae turn to ash. Beeswax begins to degrade and discolor around 85°C (185°F) and can catch fire (flashpoint) around 204°C (400°F).

Instead, the goal is to use the difference in density and state: melting the wax so it separates cleanly from the solid organic matter (slumgum). Here are the two best ways to handle this without ruining your wax.

Method 1: The Boiling Water & Strainer Method (Best for High Larvae Volume)

This is the most effective approach because boiling water keeps the temperature safely locked at 100°C (212°F), which melts the wax perfectly without burning it, while the water helps separate the larvae.

Step-by-Step Process:

  1. Bag the Comb: Place all the comb and larvae into a porous cloth bag. A burlap sack, an old pillowcase, or multiple layers of cheesecloth work perfectly. Tie the top securely.
  2. Submerge and Melt: Place the bag into a large pot of water and heat it to a gentle simmer. Do not let it hard boil. Use a heavy stone or a piece of clean scrap metal to keep the bag weighted down at the bottom of the pot.
  3. Press the Bag: As the water heats, the wax inside the comb will melt. Because liquid beeswax is less dense than water, it will seep out of the cloth bag and float to the surface. Use a heavy wooden stir stick or tongs to gently press the bag, squeezing the trapped wax out. The larvae and cocoons will remain trapped inside the cloth.
  4. Cool and Separate: Once no more wax is rising, remove the pot from the heat and let it cool completely undisturbed overnight.
  5. Harvest the Wax: The next day, you will find a solid cake of yellow beeswax floated and hardened on top of the water. The larvae and organic debris will be trapped inside the submerged bag, leaving your water muddy but your wax separated.

Method 2: The Solar Wax Extractor (Hands-Off)

If you aren't in a rush and have a string of hot, sunny days ahead, a solar wax extractor handles this automatically via gravity.

  • How it works: You place the comb on a tilted metal pan inside an insulated box with a glass lid. The sun heats the interior well past the melting point of wax ($62^\circ\text{C}$ to $64^\circ\text{C}$ / $144^\circ\text{F}$ to $147^\circ\text{F}$).
  • The separation: As the wax melts, it runs down the sloped pan, passes through a wire mesh screen (which catches the bulk of the larvae), and drips into a collection pan below. The larvae essentially dry out and remain on the upper screen as "slumgum."

Pro-Tips for Clean Wax

  • Freeze it first: If you aren't processing the comb immediately, put it in a deep freezer. Drone larvae rot incredibly fast at room temperature and will attract small hive beetles or flies within 24 hours. Freezing keeps everything solid and odorless until processing day.
  • Expect some scraping: No matter which method you use, the bottom of your final hardened wax cake will have a dark, spongy layer of fine organic debris. Simply take a paint scraper or knife and scrape this dark layer off the bottom of the cake once it cools to reveal the clean wax underneath.
  • Avoid iron or aluminum pots: Raw aluminum, iron, or copper can discolor beeswax, turning it a dull grey or greenish black. Stick to stainless steel, unchipped enamelware, or silicone containers for handling melted wax.
